hints.title: 1 · Count what each task still waits for
hints.body: For every task record how many distinct dependencies have not been placed yet, and for every task the list of tasks that wait on it. A task is ready when its count is zero. Validate every pair while you build these tables: unknown names and self-dependencies are input errors, not graph problems.

hints.title: 2 · Pull from a ready set, not a stack
hints.body: Repeatedly take the smallest ready task, append it, and decrement its followers; any follower that reaches zero becomes ready. If the output is shorter than the task list when the ready set is empty, the rest form a cycle.\n\nExample with a different problem: scheduling course prerequisites keeps `remaining[course]` and `unlocks[prerequisite]`, and a course is offered when `remaining` hits zero.

hints.title: 3 · Smallest-first needs a priority structure
hints.body: Taking `ready.min` from an array costs a scan per step, which is quadratic when every task is ready at once. Keep the ready set in a binary min-heap (push and pop are logarithmic), or keep it sorted and insert with a binary search. Test the 100,000-independent-tasks case mentally: how many comparisons does each approach make?

criteria.title: Valid order with deterministic ties
criteria.target: Every dependency is respected and the smallest ready task is chosen at every step, so the result is unique.
criteria.probe: Why does a depth-first post-order produce a valid order but fail the determinism rule?
criteria.practice: Trace the visible four-task example by hand, listing the ready set before each pick.

criteria.title: Cycles and invalid input are distinguished
criteria.target: Unknown names and self-dependencies raise ArgumentError before any ordering; a cycle raises CycleError after the ready set is exhausted.
criteria.probe: How do you know a cycle exists without searching for it explicitly?
criteria.practice: Explain what the output length tells you when the ready set empties early.

criteria.title: Near-linear cost
criteria.target: The solution is O((tasks + dependencies) log tasks); the 100,000-task groups complete in bounded time.
criteria.probe: Which single line would make your solution quadratic, and which hidden group would catch it?
criteria.practice: Replace the heap with `ready.min` and watch the independent-tasks group time out.

criteria.title: Inputs are left intact
criteria.target: Neither `tasks` nor `dependencies` is mutated; duplicate pairs are counted once.
criteria.probe: Where could an accidental `sort!` or `uniq!` sneak in, and how do you guard against it?
criteria.practice: Freeze the inputs in a scratch test and confirm nothing raises.

criteria.title: Predicted failures before running
criteria.target: Named the test a naive approach would fail and checked the prediction against the output.
criteria.probe: Before running, which group did you expect to be slowest and why?
criteria.practice: Write one expected ordering and one expected error before each run.

follow_up: Tasks now carry durations and two workers run them in parallel. Explain what a single ordering no longer determines, what you would compute instead (for example a schedule or the critical path), and where the smallest-first rule still matters. Treat this as a separate extension of the original contract.
